title: William Tell (Guillaume Tell) – Overture
hook: Dawn, a storm, a shepherd’s call and a gallop, four Alpine scenes in twelve minutes from Rossini’s last opera.

painting.title: Storm on Lake Geneva
painting.pairingNote: Boatmen fight the waves of a Swiss lake as the storm breaks and light returns on the right; in Rossini’s opera Tell is an expert boatman, forced to steer across Lake Lucerne in a storm.

facts: This is the overture to *Guillaume Tell*, Rossini’s last opera, first performed at the Paris Opéra on 3 August 1829. He was thirty-seven and at the height of his fame, and he lived almost forty more years without writing another opera.

The opera, in French, is based on Friedrich Schiller’s play *Wilhelm Tell* (1804): the legend of the Swiss archer who led his people against Austrian rule. With about four hours of music it is rarely staged complete, and the overture has become far better known than the opera itself.

It is not a medley of the opera’s tunes but a set of four connected scenes from Alpine life: dawn, a storm, a shepherd’s call, and a military gallop. Hector Berlioz, who usually disliked Rossini, called it “a symphony in four parts”.

The final gallop has had a long second life: it was the theme of *The Lone Ranger* on radio, television and film, and appears in countless cartoons and adverts. Liszt arranged the whole overture for piano in 1838.
bigPicture.inOneLine: five cellos at dawn, a mountain storm, a shepherd’s tune on the cor anglais, and a gallop led by trumpets, all without a break.

movements.heading: Andante – Allegro – Andante – Allegro vivace
movements.summary: Four scenes played without a break. A slow dawn for five solo cellos and double basses; a storm for full orchestra that builds and fades; a calm pastoral scene where a cor anglais plays a Swiss herdsman’s call; and a fast march heralded by trumpets, which ends the overture at full speed.

mainIdeas.name: Dawn
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, singing melody for a solo cello, answered by four more cellos in rich harmony, with soft timpani rolls like distant thunder.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: rushing strings, short three-note cries from the woodwinds, then the full crash of brass and bass drum.
The [[ranz-des-vaches|ranz des vaches]]: a lilting, open-air tune on the cor anglais, echoed by the flute, with a tinkling triangle.

mainIdeas.name: The gallop
mainIdeas.description: a trumpet fanfare, then a racing tune in the strings in a quick two-beat rhythm, a [[galop|galop]].

stops.hear: One cello alone, low and quiet, then the other cellos join in warm harmony
stops.happening: Dawn: five solo cellos, with the double basses below

stops.hear: Two very soft drum rolls under the cellos, like thunder far away
stops.happening: The timpani hint at the coming storm

stops.hear: The first cello climbs to a very high, held note, and the scene fades
Fast, nervous figures in the violins and violas; short three-note cries from piccolo, flute and oboes
Horns, trumpets, trombones and bass drum crash in; the whole orchestra at full force
The noise thins out, instrument by instrument, until a single flute is left
A calm, lilting tune on the cor anglais, answered by the flute; a triangle tinkles
stops.happening: The [[ranz-des-vaches|ranz des vaches]], the herdsman’s call

stops.hear: A sudden fanfare in the trumpets and horns
A racing, galloping tune in the strings; cymbals and brass join
stops.happening: The final [[galop|galop]], often called the “March of the Swiss Soldiers”

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The gallop speeds on to a string of loud closing chords

notice: Count the cellos at the start. There are five solo parts, an unusual sound for an opera overture: the orchestra begins with its darkest voices.
Listen for the flute at the end of the storm (≈ 5:00). It is the last voice left, and it leads straight into the calm.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Karajan recorded six Rossini overtures with the Berlin Philharmonic in 1971; he had recorded much the same programme in London with the Philharmonia years earlier. Here the whole overture lasts twelve minutes.

threads.title: Pictures without words
threads.body: Each part paints a scene: dawn, storm, pasture, march. It is [[programme-music|programme music]] before the word was common.

threads.title: Colour
threads.body: Rossini gives each scene its own instruments: cellos for the dawn, brass and drums for the storm, cor anglais and flute for the pasture, trumpets for the march.

threads.title: A farewell
threads.body: This was Rossini’s last opera. After it he wrote sacred music, songs and piano pieces, but never another work for the stage.
